title: Cartwell × Arize: changing the prompt safely

customer.name: Grace Liu
customer.style: a warm, articulate product manager in her late twenties on a video call, curious and a little anxious about the holiday rush

csm.name: Julian Hayes
csm.style: a friendly, confident American solutions engineer in his early thirties on a video call, clear and relaxed

lines.text: Hi Grace, good to see you. I saw your note on the booking: you want to rewrite the shopping assistant's prompt before the holidays, without breaking checkout. Let's make sure you leave today with a plan.
Exactly. The assistant is fine most days, but it rambles, and sometimes it recommends products that are out of stock. So, first question: how do we test a new prompt without shipping it?

Good question. You don't ship anything to test it. You open the Prompt Playground in Arize, paste in the new prompt, and run it against a dataset of real conversations. You see the old and the new answers side by side.
Oh, interesting. I thought the only safe way to test a prompt was to deploy every version to staging first.
No staging needed. The Playground calls the model directly with your prompt and your dataset, so production never sees it. Your engineers only get involved once you've picked a winner.
That's a relief. Where would the test conversations come from, though?

From your own traces. You filter for the conversations that went wrong, like the out of stock recommendations, add them to a dataset, and mix in some typical good ones. That way you're testing against the problems you actually have.
Makes sense. And could we try a cheaper model while we're at it?
Yes. Compare Models runs the same prompt across different models side by side, so you see quality and cost together before you switch anything.
Okay. Honestly, I'm a little nervous. If checkout breaks the week of Black Friday, that's on me.

That's completely fair, and it's exactly why you'd run it as an experiment first and only ship the winner. Then, after launch, you put monitors on what matters: latency, cost per conversation, and an eval for wrong product recommendations.
And who gets alerted if something goes wrong?
Whoever you choose. Alerts can go to email, Slack, PagerDuty or a webhook, and you can set a fixed threshold or let Arize pick one automatically from your history.
Good. One more thing: last holiday season we had a spike of bad answers. Can we compare against that?
Sure. Your Pro plan keeps a full year of traces, so last November is still in there.

Actually, let me correct myself. Pro keeps thirty days of traces, not a year, so last November is gone. Longer retention is an Enterprise option. For this season, let's save the bad holiday conversations into a dataset as we find them.
Thanks for catching that. It actually changes our plan. My VP also wants one page to look at. What would you put on it?
A dashboard. Start from a template, then add widgets like p95 latency by model, token cost, and your eval scores over time. It updates on its own, so your VP never has to ask.
Perfect. Can you send me all of this, so I can share it with the team?
Sending it now, while we're still talking.
Oh, it's here already, and it's step by step. That's great. Thanks, Julian.
Anytime. Run the first experiment this week, and let's look at the results together next Tuesday.
Sounds good. Talk then!
